submissions.findingTextShort: A human phosphatidylcholine challenge demonstrated microbiota-dependent TMAO generation, while the associated cardiovascular-risk analysis was observational rather than proof that phosphatidylcholine supplementation causes events.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 23614584 used eggs plus deuterium-labeled phosphatidylcholine to show that human TMAO production after a phosphatidylcholine challenge depends on intestinal microbiota; antibiotics suppressed the response and it returned after withdrawal. In a separate angiography cohort, higher fasting TMAO predicted major adverse cardiovascular events. The mechanistic challenge and observational risk association must remain distinct and cannot be converted into a causal cardiovascular-harm rate for phosphatidylcholine supplements.
submissions.populationContext: Healthy challenge participants plus a separate coronary-angiography cohort.
submissions.usageContext: Dietary challenge containing eggs and isotope-labeled phosphatidylcholine; not a chronic standalone supplement efficacy trial.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: TMAO association does not by itself prove phosphatidylcholine supplementation causes cardiovascular events; microbiome, diet, renal function and baseline risk are relevant boundaries.

submissions.findingTextShort: Two large US cohorts associated higher dietary phosphatidylcholine intake with higher all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, especially in diabetes, but cannot establish supplement causality.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 27281307 followed 80,978 women and 39,434 men and reported higher estimated dietary phosphatidylcholine intake was associated with higher all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, with stronger associations among participants with diabetes. This is prospective observational dietary evidence and must not be presented as proof that a phosphatidylcholine supplement causes mortality or as an individualized avoidance threshold.
submissions.populationContext: Large prospective US cohorts initially free of cancer and cardiovascular disease.
submissions.usageContext: Estimated dietary phosphatidylcholine intake, not randomized phosphatidylcholine supplementation.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Residual confounding, food-source patterns and observational design prevent causal supplement inference.

submissions.findingTextShort: A four-week randomized dietary trial found choline bitartrate raised fasting TMAO whereas the small phosphatidylcholine-supplement arm did not, providing a formulation-specific counterweight.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 33872583 randomized healthy adults with normal renal function among egg, choline-bitartrate and phosphatidylcholine interventions for four weeks. Choline-bitartrate arms significantly increased fasting TMAO, while four eggs daily and the phosphatidylcholine-supplement arm did not. The phosphatidylcholine arm was small, so this is a useful formulation-specific counterweight rather than proof that phosphatidylcholine never affects TMAO.
submissions.populationContext: Healthy adults with normal renal function; phosphatidylcholine arm n=10.
submissions.usageContext: Four-week phosphatidylcholine supplement exposure compared with other choline sources.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Small phosphatidylcholine arm and short duration limit safety inference; free choline and phosphatidylcholine cannot be treated as metabolically interchangeable exposures.

submissions.findingTextShort: Larger modified-release LT-02 ulcerative-colitis trials failed their primary induction and maintenance efficacy comparisons despite earlier favorable phase-2 evidence.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 37806372 reports two double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trials of modified-release phosphatidylcholine LT-02 in ulcerative colitis. The induction trial was terminated early for futility and showed no significant deep-remission advantage at week 12; the underpowered maintenance trial also showed no significant remission-rate difference at week 48. These later null results must remain visible beside earlier favorable delayed-release studies.
submissions.populationContext: Patients with mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis in induction and maintenance trials.
submissions.usageContext: Modified-release LT-02 formulation; disease-treatment context rather than generic oral supplement use.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Maintenance signals require confirmation and formulation-specific results cannot be generalized to all phosphatidylcholine products.

submissions.findingTextShort: A meta-analysis found favorable ulcerative-colitis outcomes for a 30% phosphatidylcholine lecithin delayed-release formulation while explicitly noting failure of a >94% formulation, reinforcing formulation non-equivalence.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: PMID 33440385 pooled three randomized trials using a 30% phosphatidylcholine-containing lecithin delayed intestinal-release formulation and reported favorable ulcerative-colitis outcomes. The review also notes that a trial using a greater-than-94% phosphatidylcholine-containing lecithin formulation failed. The evidence therefore supports a formulation-specific boundary, not a generic claim that more purified or arbitrary phosphatidylcholine treats ulcerative colitis.
submissions.populationContext: Ulcerative-colitis patients across three delayed-release formulation RCTs.
submissions.usageContext: 30% PC-containing lecithin in a delayed intestinal-release formulation; not generic standalone phosphatidylcholine.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Small evidence base, formulation dependence and later LT-02 null trials require conflicting evidence to remain visible.
